```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.2, fig.retina = 2, out.width = "100%",
                      fig.align = "center")
# Model fitting needs cmdstanr and CmdStan; without them those chunks are shown
# but not run.
has_stan <- requireNamespace("cmdstanr", quietly = TRUE) &&
  !is.null(tryCatch(cmdstanr::cmdstan_path(), error = function(e) NULL))
pal <- c(fast = "#C8553D", other = "#4F6D8F", grey = "#8C8C8C")
```

Every Gaussian model of continuous trait evolution, from Brownian motion
[@felsenstein1985] and Pagel's λ [@pagel1999] to Ornstein–Uhlenbeck
[@hansen1997; @butler2004], early-burst [@blomberg2003; @harmon2010] and
multi-rate models [@omeara2006; @eastman2011; @venditti2011], says the
same thing about the data:

$$ y \sim \mathcal{N}(X\beta,\; K), $$

and the models differ only in the covariance matrix $K$, the **kernel**.
In `phylogp` you build a model by adding kernel components, and the package
writes, compiles and fits the corresponding Stan program.

This tutorial walks through a complete analysis of simulated data in which
one clade evolves much faster than the rest of the tree. We will

1. look at what different kernels assume,
2. fit the classical models by maximum likelihood,
3. fit a *relaxed-rate* kernel that lets the rate of evolution itself
   evolve along the tree, and compare models by leave-one-out
   cross-validation, and
4. map the estimated rates back onto the tree.

## Simulated data: a clade that evolves fast

We simulate a time-calibrated tree of 100 species, scaled to height 1, and
pick a clade of about 20 species.

```{r tree}
library(phylogp)
set.seed(13)

tr <- ape::rphylo(100, birth = 1, death = 0)     # a pure-birth tree
tr$edge.length <- tr$edge.length / max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(tr))

N <- ape::Ntip(tr)
clade_sizes <- lengths(ape::prop.part(tr))       # tips below each internal node
fast_node <- N + which.min(abs(clade_sizes - 20))

descendants <- function(node) {
  kids <- tr$edge[tr$edge[, 1] == node, 2]
  c(node, unlist(lapply(kids, descendants)))
}
in_clade <- descendants(fast_node)
fast_tips <- tr$tip.label[intersect(in_clade, seq_len(N))]
length(fast_tips)
```

Within that clade, a trait evolves 8 times faster than elsewhere. We
express this with the log-rate path `z` used by `k_relaxed()`: the rate of
an edge is `exp((z_start + z_end) / 2)`, so setting `z = log(8)` on every
node of the clade gives an 8-fold rate inside it.

The response, say brain size, scales with body size (slope 0.7) and has a
residual that evolves with these rates, plus a little species-level noise.

```{r simulate}
z <- numeric(N + tr$Nnode)
z[in_clade] <- log(8)
true_rates <- exp(0.5 * (z[tr$edge[, 1]] + z[tr$edge[, 2]]))

body  <- kernel_simulate(k_bm(), tr, pars = list(bm1 = list(sigma = 1.5)))[, 1]
resid <- kernel_simulate(k_relaxed() + k_white(), tr,
                         pars = list(relaxed1 = list(sigma = 1, z = z),
                                     white1   = list(sigma = 0.1)))[, 1]
d <- data.frame(body = body, brain = 0.5 + 0.7 * body + resid[names(body)])
head(d)
```

```{r plot-data, fig.height = 4.6}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot_tree_rates(tr, true_rates, lim = 3, main = "True rate of evolution")
fast <- rownames(d) %in% fast_tips
plot(brain ~ body, data = d, pch = 21, cex = 1.2,
     bg = adjustcolor(ifelse(fast, pal["fast"], pal["other"]), 0.75),
     col = "white", las = 1, bty = "l", xlab = "log body size",
     ylab = "log brain size", main = "Species data", font.main = 1)
legend("topleft", c("fast clade", "other species"), pt.bg = pal[1:2],
       pch = 21, col = "white", pt.cex = 1.2, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

## What does a kernel assume?

Before fitting anything, `kernel_plot()` shows the correlation between
species that a kernel implies. Tips are in the same order in the tree and in
the matrix, so clades appear as blocks.

```{r kernel-bm, fig.height = 4.6}
kernel_plot(k_bm() + k_white(), tr,
            pars = list(white1 = list(sigma = 0.5)),
            main = "Brownian motion + residual")
```

An Ornstein–Uhlenbeck kernel with strong selection forgets deep history:
only close relatives remain correlated.

```{r kernel-ou, fig.height = 4.6}
kernel_plot(k_ou(), tr, pars = list(ou1 = list(alpha = 4)),
            main = "Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (alpha = 4)")
```

## Classical models by maximum likelihood

With `method = "optimize"`, `phylo_gp()` finds maximum-likelihood
estimates; for the classical kernels these agree with `phylolm` to
numerical precision.

```{r ml, eval = has_stan, message = FALSE}
classical <- list(BM = k_bm(), "Pagel's lambda" = k_lambda(),
                  OU = k_ou(), "Early burst" = k_eb())
ml <- lapply(classical, function(k)
  phylo_gp(brain ~ body, data = d, tree = tr, kernel = k, method = "optimize"))

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  logLik = sapply(ml, function(f) as.numeric(logLik(f))),
  AIC    = sapply(ml, AIC),
  slope  = sapply(ml, function(f) coef(f)[["body"]])
), digits = 2)
```

All four overestimate the slope (the true value is 0.7): none of them can
represent a rate that differs between clades, so the large residuals of the
fast clade, whose species sit at the upper end of body size, pull the
regression line upwards.

## A kernel whose rate evolves

`k_relaxed()` lets the log rate of evolution follow a Brownian motion along
the tree, without being told where any shift lies, much as relaxed-clock
models let rates of molecular evolution vary [@thorne2002]; related
approaches for continuous traits include variable-rates models
[@eastman2011; @venditti2011; @revell2021multirate] and relaxed random walks
[@fisher2021relaxed]. Its rates are latent
variables, so it is fitted by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. We compare it with
the Bayesian version of the Pagel's λ model (BM plus residual).

```{r bayes, eval = has_stan, message = FALSE}
fit_bm      <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, data = d, tree = tr,
                        kernel = k_bm() + k_white(), seed = 1)
fit_relaxed <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, data = d, tree = tr,
                        kernel = k_relaxed() + k_white(), seed = 1)
fit_relaxed
```

`relaxed1_tau`, the standard deviation of log-rate change, is clearly above
zero: the data favour variable rates.

Leave-one-out cross-validation [@vehtari2017] asks which model predicts each species
better from all the others. `phylogp` computes the exact conditional
densities $p(y_i \mid y_{-i}, \theta)$ in linear time, and `loo()` combines
them across posterior draws.

```{r loo, eval = has_stan}
loo::loo_compare(list("BM + residual"      = loo(fit_bm),
                      "relaxed + residual" = loo(fit_relaxed)))
```

The relaxed-rate kernel predicts left-out species clearly better, and its
slope estimate is close to the true 0.7. The flags report species with
Pareto $\hat k > 0.7$, for which the importance-sampling approximation is
unreliable; these are influential species, often in the fast clade. In a
real analysis, recompute their contributions exactly by refitting without
them before drawing conclusions.

## Where did the rate change?

`plot_edge_rates()` colours every branch by its posterior median rate,
relative to a typical branch.

```{r rates, eval = has_stan, fig.height = 4.8}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot_tree_rates(tr, true_rates, lim = 3, main = "True rates")
plot_edge_rates(fit_relaxed, lim = 3, main = "Estimated rates (posterior median)")
par(op)
```

The fast clade is recovered without any prior information about its
location. `edge_rates()` returns the numbers, with 90% intervals:

```{r rates-ci, eval = has_stan, fig.height = 4}
er <- edge_rates(fit_relaxed)
ft <- fit_relaxed$tree
er$fast <- er$child %in% in_clade
er <- er[order(er$median), ]

op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(seq_len(nrow(er)), er$median, log = "y", type = "n", las = 1, bty = "l",
     ylim = range(er$q5, er$q95), xlab = "branches, ordered by estimated rate",
     ylab = "relative rate (log scale)")
segments(seq_len(nrow(er)), er$q5, y1 = er$q95,
         col = adjustcolor(ifelse(er$fast, pal["fast"], pal["other"]), 0.5), lwd = 2)
points(seq_len(nrow(er)), er$median, pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
       col = ifelse(er$fast, pal["fast"], pal["other"]))
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = pal["grey"])
legend("topleft", c("branches in the fast clade", "other branches"),
       col = pal[1:2], pch = 19, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

The autocorrelated prior smooths an abrupt shift, so the size of the
change is underestimated (the truth is 8-fold) even though its location is
found. This is the expected behaviour of the model, and the reason to
read the estimated ratio as conservative.

## Several observations per species

Data often come as individuals rather than species means [@ives2007]. Give the column
of species names in `species` and keep one row per individual: the kernel
then describes the species, a `k_white()` component becomes the
non-phylogenetic species effect, and a residual standard deviation within
species (`within_sigma`) is added. The likelihood is exact and still linear
in the number of species, because it factorises into the species means and
the deviations from them. Here we sample two to six individuals per
species, with body size varying within species:

```{r individuals, eval = has_stan, message = FALSE}
set.seed(7)
ind <- data.frame(species = rep(rownames(d), sample(2:6, N, replace = TRUE)))
dev_body  <- rnorm(nrow(ind), 0, 0.2)
ind$body  <- d[ind$species, "body"] + dev_body
ind$brain <- d[ind$species, "brain"] + 0.7 * dev_body + rnorm(nrow(ind), 0, 0.3)
nrow(ind)

fit_ind <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, data = ind, tree = tr,
                    kernel = k_bm() + k_white(), species = "species",
                    method = "optimize")
fit_ind
```

Leave-one-out cross-validation then leaves out whole species, and
`predict()` with `type = "response"` predicts a new individual.

## Under the hood

Each kernel component adds its contribution to the variance accumulated
along every branch. When all components have this branch-wise form, the
likelihood is evaluated by the linear-time pruning recursion
[@felsenstein1973; @ho2014]. You can
inspect, and edit, the generated program:

```{r code, eval = has_stan}
code <- strsplit(kernel_stancode(fit_relaxed), "\n")[[1]]
cat(code[grep("^model", code):(grep("^generated", code) - 1)], sep = "\n")
```

Called on a kernel instead of a fit, `kernel_stancode()` produces the same program without fitting, and
`kernel_standata()` the matching data, so a model can be taken further in
`cmdstanr` directly.
